newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Unilever, Mars resume fight over ice-cream.
newsitem.headline: Unilever, Mars resume fight over ice-cream.

text.p: The European Commission sent a fresh warning to Unilever Plc on Friday over the way it sells ice-cream bars in Ireland, an issue which has put the Anglo- Dutch consumer goods giant at loggerheads with rival Mars Inc.

The Commission said it was sending Unilever a so-called statement of objections after it became clear that changes propsoed by the company aimed at loosening its grip on retailers in Ireland failed to open up the market to competition.

The row is about the practice by which Unilever, but also Mars and other ice-cream giants, virtually tie up shops by providing free freezer cabinets to store so-called "impulse ice-cream", provided they are used exclusively for their products, not the competitors'.
The practice is worldwide, but Ireland is being used as a test case. Impulse ice-cream is products sold at small outlets for immediate consumption.

In 1991 and 1992, the Commission received complaints from Masterfoods Ireland Ltd, a Mars company, and Valley Ice Cream Ltd relating to the distribution arrangements operated by Unilever's Irish subsidiary HB Ice Cream Ltd, now trading as Van den Bergh Foods Ltd.
This followed Unilever's legal action against Mars in Ireland for allegedly enticing retailers to breach the contract of exclusivity.
The Commission agreed in 1995 to drop the case after Unilever proposed giving retailers the option of gradually buying its cabinets to give them the choice of the products they could sell.

But this produced little results, the Commission said in a statement. "While...a number of Unilever's older cabinets have been sold in an attempt to encourage a move toward cabinet ownership, the option of hire purchasing freezer cabinets has proved unattractive," it said.
The Commission did not say what it might do next, but Unilever's spokesman Tom Gordijn hoped it would accept that freezer exclusivity is a good practice.
"We hope we will be able to convince the Commission that the favourable position taken in March 1995 can be sustained," he told Reuters.
The Commission's latest move was also closely watched by Mars UK managing director Simon Bullimore, who wished for "a speedy conclusion to the case".
But when this will happen is unsure. The fight has already been going on for more than six years and it is likely to last another six to eight months, Commission sources said
